prompt: After fork(), how do parent and child differ in return value and memory, and is memory actually copied?
reveal: Gist: `fork()` clones the calling process into a near-identical child, and its **return value** is how each side learns which one it is — the parent gets back the child's **PID** (process ID, the kernel's number for the new process), the child gets `0`, and `-1` means the fork failed. The child receives a copy of the parent's **address space** — its entire memory image — but the copy is lazy, not upfront: modern kernels use **copy-on-write**, meaning parent and child share the same physical pages marked read-only, and the kernel only duplicates a page at the moment one side actually **writes** to it. **Tell:** the memory you “get” from fork costs nothing until you touch it.

prompt: Explain the three-level file-descriptor model: the per-process fd table, the open file table, and the inode table. Why does this structure make dup() and fork() behave the way they do?

src.ref: §5.4 Relationship between file descriptors and open files

reveal:
Gist: a file descriptor is just a small integer, but behind it the kernel stacks **three** tables — and that layering is exactly what explains why some open files share a position and others don't.

The three levels: (1) the **per-process fd table** — one table per process, indexed by the fd number you hold; each entry points to (2) an **open file description** — a system-wide object that holds the current **file offset** (where the next read or write lands) and the **status flags** (how the file was opened, e.g. read-only, append); which in turn points to (3) the **inode** — the kernel's record of the actual file on disk.

Now the payoff. `dup()` (which copies a descriptor) and `fork()` (which copies a whole process) both duplicate the **fd-table entry**, but the copy still points at the **same** open file description. So the two descriptors **share one offset**: a write through one advances the position seen by the other. Contrast two independent `open()` calls on the same file — each builds its **own** open file description, so each gets a **separate** offset that moves independently.

**Tell:** shared offset means a shared open file description (from `dup`/`fork`); independent offset means separate `open()` calls.

prompt: You must handle 10k concurrent sockets. Why do select()/poll() scale poorly, and what does epoll change? Contrast level- vs edge-triggered.
reveal:
Gist: to watch 10,000 sockets efficiently you want the kernel to hand you only the ones that are ready — not make you re-scan all 10,000 every time.

`select()` and `poll()` are **O(n)** in the number of watched descriptors: on **every** call you pass the entire descriptor set into the kernel, and the kernel scans all of it to find the ready ones. So cost grows with the **total** number of connections even when only a handful are active — the wasted work is the whole set minus the few that matter.

**epoll** flips this. You register your interest set **once** in a kernel data structure, then each wait returns **only the descriptors that are ready** — **O(ready)**, not O(total). That's what makes tens of thousands of mostly-idle connections practical.

Two readiness modes. **Level-triggered** fires as long as data remains — the forgiving, `poll`-like default: if you don't read everything this time, you'll be told again. **Edge-triggered** fires **once**, only on a readiness **transition** (not-ready → ready), so you must **drain** the descriptor completely — keep reading until you get `EAGAIN` (the “nothing left right now” error) — or you lose the event and hang waiting for a notification that never repeats. Edge is faster (fewer wakeups) but far easier to get wrong.

prompt: Walk through fork() and exec(). What does copy-on-write do, and what does fork return?

src.ref: Ch.24 Process Creation; Ch.27 Program Execution

reveal:
Gist: `fork()` makes a copy of the running process, and `exec()` throws away that copy's program and loads a new one in its place — the two together are how every new program gets launched on Unix.

`fork()` creates a near-identical **child** process. Its **return value** is how the two branches tell themselves apart: it returns the child's **PID** (process ID) in the parent and `0` in the child (`-1` on failure). **Copy-on-write** means the child's address space isn't really duplicated up front — parent and child share the same physical pages marked read-only, and only when one side **writes** does the kernel copy that single page. So the fork is cheap; you pay only for what you actually modify.

`exec()` then **replaces the process image entirely** — the old program's code and data are gone, swapped for the new program — while **keeping the same PID and the open file descriptors**. That inheritance is exactly how a shell sets up redirection: it `fork`s, rearranges the child's descriptors (point stdout at a file, say), and only **then** `exec`s the target program, which starts up already wired to the right files.

prompt: What is a file descriptor, and what actually happens to descriptors across fork and exec?
reveal:
Gist: a file descriptor is a small integer handle, and what happens to it across `fork` and `exec` is the whole reason pipes and shell redirection work.

Concretely, a **file descriptor** is a small integer that indexes the process's **descriptor table**; each entry points to an **open file description** (a kernel object holding the **file offset** — where the next read/write lands — and the status flags), which in turn points to an **inode**, the kernel's record of the real file.

Across **`fork`**, the child gets a **copy** of the descriptor table, but the copies point at the **same** open file descriptions — so parent and child **share the file offset**, which is why their interleaved writes to the same descriptor land in a surprising, intermixed order.

Across **`exec`**, descriptors **survive by default** — the new program inherits them — which is precisely how pipes and redirection keep working after the program is replaced. When you *don't* want that inheritance, set the **`FD_CLOEXEC`** flag (“close on exec”) on the descriptor, or open it with **`O_CLOEXEC`** in the first place, and the kernel closes it automatically at the next `exec`.

prompt: How does a shell implement `a | b`? Describe the syscall sequence.
reveal:
Gist: a shell wires `a | b` by creating a pipe, forking both programs, and redirecting `a`'s output and `b`'s input into the two ends of that pipe.

Step by step. Call **`pipe()`** to get two connected descriptors — a **read end** and a **write end**; bytes written to one come out the other. **`fork()` twice**, once per program. In the **first child** (which will run `a`): `dup2(writeEnd, STDOUT_FILENO)` so its standard output *becomes* the pipe's write end, then close both original pipe descriptors, then `exec` `a`. In the **second child** (which will run `b`): `dup2(readEnd, STDIN_FILENO)` so its standard input becomes the pipe's read end, close the originals, `exec` `b`.

The crucial part: the **parent must close BOTH ends** of the pipe. A reader only sees **EOF** (end of file — the signal that no more data is coming) once **every** write end, in **every** process, is closed. A single forgotten open write end — often one the parent itself still holds — means the reader waits forever for an EOF that never arrives. That leftover descriptor is the classic reason a pipeline **hangs**.

prompt: What is a signal, and what makes writing a signal handler dangerous?
reveal:
Gist: a signal is an **asynchronous** interruption — the kernel can pause your program at almost any instruction to run a handler — and that “almost any instruction” is exactly what makes handlers treacherous.

A **signal** is a notification delivered to a process out of nowhere, not tied to your program's own flow: `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C), `SIGTERM` (polite kill request), `SIGSEGV` (bad memory access), `SIGCHLD` (a child process changed state). When one arrives, the kernel can suspend the program **mid-instruction** and jump into your handler.

The danger: that handler might fire in the **middle** of a `malloc` or a `printf`, then call the same function again — re-entering **non-reentrant** code (code that assumes it's never interrupted partway through) and corrupting its internal bookkeeping or deadlocking on a lock it already holds. So a handler may only call **async-signal-safe** functions — the specific set guaranteed safe to run in this interrupted context. `write` is safe; `printf` and `malloc` are **not**.

**The standard safe pattern:** don't do real work in the handler. Just set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag (a variable type guaranteed to be updated in one uninterruptible step), or write a single byte to a **self-pipe** or **eventfd** (a descriptor your main loop is already watching), and let the **main loop** notice and do the actual work back in normal context.

prompt: Contrast select, poll, and epoll. What makes epoll scale, and what is edge- vs level-triggered?
reveal:
Gist: `select` and `poll` make you re-hand the kernel your entire watch list on every call; `epoll` registers it once and returns only what's ready — which is what lets one thread ride herd on 100,000 connections.

`select` and `poll` require passing the **entire** descriptor set into the kernel on **every** call, and the kernel scans all of it — **O(n)** per call in the number watched. `select` has an extra limit: it can't watch beyond **`FD_SETSIZE`** descriptors (typically 1024).

`epoll` registers your interest **once** in a kernel data structure, then each wait returns **only the ready descriptors** — **O(ready)** rather than O(total). That shift from “rescan everything” to “report only the ready ones” is what makes 100k concurrent connections viable.

Two notification modes. **Level-triggered** reports readiness **as long as data remains** — forgiving, `poll`-like semantics: miss some this round and you'll be reminded next round. **Edge-triggered** reports **only on a state change** (not-ready → ready), fired once, so you must **drain the socket until `EAGAIN`** (the “nothing left for now” error) or you'll hang waiting for an event that never repeats. Edge-triggered is faster — fewer wakeups — but the classic source of subtle, hard-to-find bugs.

prompt: What does mmap do, and when is it better or worse than read/write?
reveal:
Gist: `mmap` makes a file look like a chunk of your process's memory, so you read and write it with ordinary pointer accesses instead of `read`/`write` system calls.

Mechanically, `mmap` maps a file — or plain anonymous memory backed by nothing — into the process's **address space**. Touching that memory then triggers **demand paging** (the kernel pulls in each page on first access via a page fault) instead of an explicit syscall per operation.

**Better when:** you do **random access** into a large file (no syscall on every access), you want to **share memory** between processes (they map the same file), or you want to **avoid the copy** from a kernel buffer into a user buffer that `read`/`write` performs.

**Worse when:** you're **streaming sequentially** — a `read` into a large buffer is comparable in speed and simpler; the file is **smaller than a page** — mapping overhead dominates; or you need **precise error handling** — an I/O error surfaces as a **`SIGBUS`** signal at the moment you touch the page, rather than as a return code you can check. It also makes **page-fault latency unpredictable** (any access might block to fetch a page), which matters on latency-critical paths.

prompt: A process shows high VIRT but low RSS. Explain the difference between virtual size, RSS, and shared memory.

src.ref: Ch.6 Processes (memory layout of a process); Ch.49 Memory Mappings

reveal:
Gist: a process can **reserve** a huge address space while only a little of it is actually in RAM — that gap between reserved and resident is the whole point of the VIRT-versus-RSS distinction.

**VIRT (virtual size)** is the **total address space the process has reserved** — including memory it allocated but never touched, mapped files, and every shared library it links. Reserving costs only **page-table entries**, not physical RAM, which is why VIRT can be enormous and mostly meaningless.

**RSS (resident set size)** is the **physical RAM actually backing those pages right now**, shared pages included.

The catch with RSS: it **counts shared libraries and shared memory in full inside every process that maps them**. So if you **sum** RSS across all processes, the shared pages get **double-counted**, and the total can exceed the machine's real RAM — a common source of confusion. **PSS (proportional set size)** fixes this by **dividing each shared page's cost among the processes sharing it**, giving an honest per-process number that actually adds up.

prompt: What is memory overcommit and the OOM killer? Why can malloc succeed and the write still crash?

src.ref: Ch.7 Memory Allocation; Ch.49 Memory Mappings (overcommit and the OOM killer)

reveal:
Gist: Linux hands out memory it doesn't actually have yet, betting you won't use all of it — so `malloc` can say “yes” and the machine can still run out when you finally **write** to that memory.

By default Linux **overcommits**: it grants **virtual** address space without reserving matching **physical** pages, gambling that most programs never touch everything they allocate. So `malloc` succeeds just by adjusting the process's mappings — no RAM is set aside. Physical pages are assigned only on **first touch** (the first read or write to each page). If RAM happens to be exhausted at that moment, the kernel invokes the **OOM killer** (out-of-memory killer), which picks a victim process by its **`oom_score`** — roughly its memory footprint, adjusted by the tunable **`oom_score_adj`** — and kills it.

That's the answer to the paradox: a **write** to freshly `malloc`'d memory can die even though `malloc` returned a non-null pointer — because the pointer only ever promised address space, and the page behind it wasn't real until you touched it.

**Control it:** tune overcommit policy via `/proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory`, or in a latency-critical process **pre-touch** every page and **`mlock`** it (lock it into RAM) so the pages are real and can never be reclaimed or fault mid-operation.

prompt: What is /proc, and name five things you would actually read from it while debugging.
reveal:
Gist: `/proc` looks like a directory of files, but there's no disk behind it — each “file” is a live window the kernel generates on read, exposing its own state and every process's state as plain text.

It's a **virtual filesystem**: reading a path under `/proc` makes the kernel materialize the answer on the spot. Five things worth reading while debugging:

- **`/proc/<pid>/status`** — memory use, thread count, and voluntary/involuntary context-switch counts (is the process getting starved of CPU?).
- **`/proc/<pid>/maps`** — the full address-space layout: which ranges map which libraries and regions. Match a segfault's faulting address against this to see what it hit.
- **`/proc/<pid>/fd/`** — every open file and socket, as symlinks. This is how you catch a **descriptor leak** (the count only ever climbing).
- **`/proc/<pid>/stack`** or **`/proc/<pid>/wchan`** — where a **hung** process is blocked inside the kernel (which function it's parked in).
- **`/proc/meminfo`** and **`/proc/interrupts`** — system-wide memory pressure, and how interrupts are distributed across CPUs.

prompt: When do you reach for strace, ltrace, perf, and gdb? Pick the tool for: a program that hangs.
reveal:
Gist: match the tool to the layer where the bug lives — the kernel boundary, library calls, CPU time, or program logic.

- **`strace`** traces **system calls** — every request your program makes to the kernel. Reach for it when the program interacts with the OS wrongly (a missing file, a `read` that blocks, a permission denial), and especially for a **hang**, because it shows the exact syscall the program is stuck inside.
- **`ltrace`** traces **library calls** instead of syscalls — occasionally handy, rarely the tool you need.
- **`perf`** is a **sampling profiler** for **CPU-bound** problems: where time actually goes, plus cache misses and branch mispredictions.
- **`gdb`** is the **debugger** for logic bugs and crashes; you can also attach it to a running process with `gdb -p <pid>` and run `thread apply all bt` to dump every thread's call stack.

**For a hang specifically:** start with `strace` — is it blocked in a syscall? If `strace` shows **nothing**, the process is spinning in user code rather than waiting on the kernel, so switch to `gdb -p` to see the full picture of where it's looping.

prompt: TCP vs UDP: state the guarantees and when a low-latency system deliberately chooses UDP.

src.ref: Ch.58 Sockets: Fundamentals of TCP/IP Networks; Ch.59 Internet Domain Sockets

reveal:
Gist: TCP is a reliable ordered pipe that guarantees delivery at the cost of delay; UDP is a fire-and-forget message service that trades all those guarantees for the lowest possible latency.

**TCP** gives an **ordered, reliable, connection-oriented byte stream** — bytes arrive in order, with none lost, over a connection you set up first — plus **congestion control** (backing off when the network is full) and **flow control** (not overrunning a slow receiver). The price: **head-of-line blocking** (one lost packet stalls everything queued behind it while TCP retransmits), retransmission delay, and connection-setup cost.

**UDP** is an **unreliable, unordered datagram service** — discrete messages that may be dropped, duplicated, or reordered — with essentially **no overhead**.

Low-latency systems deliberately choose **UDP (usually multicast)** for things like **market data** because a **retransmitted stale price is worthless** — you'd rather drop it and take the next update than wait for the old one to be resent — and **multicast** delivers a single send to many receivers at once. The application protocol then adds **sequence numbers** to detect gaps and reordering itself, keeping only the guarantees it actually needs.

prompt: What is Nagle’s algorithm and delayed ACK, and why is their interaction a latency trap?

src.ref: Ch.61 Sockets: Advanced Topics (TCP_NODELAY / the Nagle algorithm)

reveal:
Gist: two separate TCP optimizations — one on the sender, one on the receiver — are each reasonable alone, but together they can stall a request/response exchange for ~40 milliseconds.

**Nagle's algorithm** lives on the **sender**: it **buffers small writes** until the previously sent data has been acknowledged, so a chatty program can't flood the network with tiny one-byte packets. **Delayed ACK** lives on the **receiver**: it **waits** (up to ~40 ms) before sending an acknowledgment, hoping to **piggyback** that ACK onto an outgoing response and save a packet.

Put them together and they **briefly deadlock**: the sender is holding its small write, waiting for an **ACK** before it sends more; the receiver is holding that ACK, waiting for a **response** to attach it to. Neither moves until the receiver's ~40 ms delayed-ACK timer finally expires — producing periodic **40 ms latency spikes** on exactly the request/response protocols where latency matters most.

**The fix:** set **`TCP_NODELAY`** on the socket to disable Nagle, so small writes go out immediately. It's standard practice in any latency-sensitive service.

prompt: What is CPU affinity and why do latency-critical systems pin threads? What else gets tuned alongside it?
reveal:
Gist: **CPU affinity** nails a thread to specific cores so the scheduler can't move it around — because every move throws away the caches that were making it fast.

You set affinity with **`sched_setaffinity`** (or the `taskset` command), **binding** a thread to a chosen core or set of cores; the scheduler is then forbidden to **migrate** it elsewhere. Migration is expensive: the thread lands on a new core with a **cold L1/L2 cache** and a **cold branch predictor** (both were warmed up on the old core and don't come along), so it stalls while they refill — a latency spike. Pinning keeps the thread's **working set hot** on one core.

Pinning alone isn't enough, so latency-critical systems tune around it: **`isolcpus`** or **cgroup cpusets** to keep *other* work off those cores; **IRQ affinity** to move device interrupts onto separate housekeeping cores so they don't interrupt the hot thread; **disabling hyperthreading** on the isolated cores so a sibling thread can't contend for the same physical core; and setting the **CPU governor to `performance`** so the clock frequency doesn't drop during brief idle gaps and leave you slow at the next burst.

prompt: Static vs dynamic linking: what is the runtime cost of dynamic linking, and is it only at startup?
reveal:
Gist: dynamic linking defers wiring your program to its libraries until run time, and that convenience costs you both at startup **and** on every cross-library call — which is why latency-obsessed shops often link statically instead.

**Dynamic linking** resolves symbols (matches each function name to its address) at **load time**, or **lazily** on the first call via the **PLT** (Procedure Linkage Table, the little trampoline that stands in for a not-yet-resolved function). So startup pays for **relocation** and **symbol lookup** across every shared object.

And it's **not** only at startup. Every call into a shared library goes through **PLT/GOT indirection** (the GOT, Global Offset Table, holds the resolved address the trampoline jumps to) — an extra hop that **can't be inlined across the library boundary**, so the optimizer can't fuse caller and callee. Lazy binding also means the **first** call to each function pays a one-time resolver round trip.

**Static linking** bakes the library code straight into the executable, eliminating both costs: it enables **cross-module inlining** and **LTO** (link-time optimization, whole-program optimization across what were separate files) and gives **more predictable latency**. That's why HFT binaries are often **statically linked** — accepting a larger binary and the loss of shared-library security/bug updates in exchange for speed and predictability.

prompt: Which command shows you: open file descriptors of a process, listening sockets, and per-CPU interrupt counts?
reveal: Three quick diagnostics, one command each. **Open file descriptors** of a process: `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` or `lsof -p <pid>`. **Listening sockets:** `ss -ltnp` — the modern replacement for `netstat -ltnp` (l = listening, t = TCP, n = numeric ports, p = show the owning process). **Per-CPU interrupt counts:** `cat /proc/interrupts`, which breaks down interrupts by source and CPU — use it to confirm NIC interrupts are landing on the cores you intended rather than all piling onto CPU0. **Tell:** descriptors live under `/proc/<pid>/fd`; `ss` supersedes `netstat`.
